docs.title: lvgl-mpy-linux
docs.text:
Turn a Linux board into a MicroPython board with a touch screen, where the GUI and the operating system work as one. Write the GUI in Python with LVGL, use mpremote as on any MicroPython board, and let every button reach what Linux can do: files, network, audio, GPIO, and every program the board can run.

Weather: five days, drawn icons, night dimming

Web radio: internet stations

MP3 player: songs from the SD card

Settings: Wi-Fi for every app

All these apps were built with LVGL MPY Studio through its MCP tools: an AI assistant designed the screens, wrote the code, tried it in the Studio's simulator and ran it on the board.

Status: mp135-v0.1. One board tested, the STM32MP135F-DK. A personal, experimental project for makers, not affiliated with, sponsored or endorsed by any of the manufacturers of the boards and chips it uses; their names only identify the hardware.

docs.title: Why: the GUI and the operating system, together
docs.text:
On a Linux board the graphical app and the system usually live apart. On one side a GUI toolkit (Qt, GTK, a web page), on the other the programs and services of the system; between them, glue in C++, D-Bus or shell scripts. That glue is where most makers stop.

lvgl-mpy-linux puts the GUI inside the system. The screen is LVGL, written in Python, and the same Python code reaches everything Linux can do:

A touch on the screen... ...uses the operating system plays a song or an internet radio gst-play-1.0 (GStreamer), driven while it plays shows the weather of the next days curl in the background, the system clock connects to a Wi-Fi network wpa_supplicant and systemd-networkd, configured the standard way runs a command, edits a file a shell with real Linux programs on a pseudo-terminal switches a LED, reads a button the kernel's GPIO lines (machine.Pin) powers the board off systemctl poweroff

And it works the other way round: the programs answer, and the GUI follows them live (the position of a song, the state of the network, the output of a command) without ever freezing, because the slow work runs in the background.

It is made for makers, so it keeps what makes microcontrollers easy:

  • The workflow of a MicroPython board. A REPL on USB serial and TCP that mpremote and LVGL MPY Studio use as on any board (raw REPL, cp, run, mount), Ctrl-C, a soft reset in 0.2 s, safe mode on a button. No compositor, no cross-compiled C++, no image to rebuild for an app.
  • The same app on MCU and Linux. The display_driver interface is the one of the MCU boards of mpy-lvgl-boards: an app for an RP2350 or an ESP32 runs unchanged on a Linux board with a bigger screen, and can then grow into Linux.
  • An appliance, not a desktop. At power-on a shell on the display; a tap opens a menu of apps (weather, radio) and power off. The board becomes a device you build.
  • Apps written with an assistant, and checked. LVGL MPY Studio's MCP tools let an AI assistant write the glue between the GUI and the system; the simulator and the tests on the board check it.

docs.title: LVGL MPY Studio and its MCP tools
docs.text:
LVGL MPY Studio designs LVGL screens by drag and drop, runs them in a simulator and uploads them to the board. Import the board definition (studio-board/boards/stm32mp135f_dk_480x272.json) in its board manager and the Linux board is one more target.

The Studio also offers its tools through MCP, so an AI coding assistant can build a whole application: add pages and widgets, write handlers and Python modules, render the pages, play touch scripts in the simulator, upload to the board and read its console. That is how the examples here were made.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
PC: LVGL MPY Studio / mpremote
        │ USB serial (CDC-ACM)        │ TCP over USB network
        └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                 mpy-repl-hub            one REPL for both, Ctrl-C as a signal, systemd watchdog
                       │ pseudo-terminal
     MicroPython unix port + LVGL 9.5    REPL like the MCU ports, soft reset by execve
       ├── display_driver ── linuxfb ──── DRM panel
       │                  └─ touch_evdev ─ touchscreen
       ├── machine.Pin ─────────────────── GPIO character device
       └── linuxproc ───────────────────── Linux programs (gst-play, curl, shell, ...)

MicroPython, LVGL and the LVGL binding are used unchanged: everything is an out-of-tree variant, user C modules and frozen Python.

docs.title: Boards
docs.text:
Board Status STM32MP135F-DK (480×272, OpenSTLinux) Tested: build, installation, REPL, display, touch, GPIO, Wi-Fi, examples STM32MP157C-DK2 (800×480, with a Cortex-M4) Working: the same build, examples, Wi-Fi, sound; machine.I2C, ADC, PWM, SPI, UART and Timer served by the Cortex-M4 over RPMsg (notes) Other Linux boards The Linux parts are generic; a port needs a build for its CPU

What a Linux board needs: a panel the kernel drives through DRM, a touchscreen through evdev, and a USB device port for the serial REPL (or only the network for the TCP REPL).

docs.title: What's next: the machine class, above all with an MCU on board
docs.text:
machine offers Pin on the kernel's GPIO lines and, on the STM32MP157C-DK2, I2C, ADC, PWM, SPI, UART and Timer served by its Cortex-M4. The plan is to port the rest of the MicroPython machine API (WDT, Pin.irq) with the same names and behaviour as on the MCU ports, so that hardware code moves between boards unchanged.

A board that pairs Linux with a microcontroller gets the best of both: Python and the GUI on Linux, the real-time work on the MCU. On the STM32MP157C-DK2 machine talks to our firmware on the Cortex-M4 over RPMsg (about 0.3 ms a request: measured latency), so a Python app reads sensors with microcontroller timing while Linux keeps the screen, the network and the programs. On boards without an MCU the same classes will use the kernel's drivers. See the STM32MP157C-DK2.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Honestly, today:

  • Two boards tested, both STM32MP1. The parts for other Linux boards are written but not tried on one yet.
  • Start-up takes about 33 s on the stock OpenSTLinux image.
  • machine has Pin, and I2C, ADC, PWM, SPI, UART and Timer on the STM32MP157C-DK2, for now: see what's next above.
  • No vsync: fast full-screen animations can tear.
  • The TCP REPL has no password: it listens only on the USB network.

MicroPython, LVGL and the LVGL binding of PyDevices do the hard work. MIT license.

docs.title: The display_driver contract on the STM32MP135F-DK
docs.text: python/linux/display_driver.py implements version 1 of the display_driver contract (CONTRACT = 1) defined in docs/display-driver.md of mpy-lvgl-boards: the same names (WIDTH, HEIGHT, BUFFERS, PERIOD_MS, indev, start(), stop(), running(), backlight()) as on the MCU boards, so code generated by LVGL MPY Studio does not know that it runs on Linux.

docs.title: Linux backend
docs.text:
The Linux driver uses a DRM dumb buffer and the Goodix event device. It has one full-screen RGB565 buffer in DIRECT mode and exposes the measured panel resolution and stride through linuxfb.open(). The backlight maps 0–100% to the kernel sysfs brightness range. stop() waits for the LVGL thread to finish; calling it from an LVGL callback in that same thread does not wait for itself. start() cannot overlap an earlier service that is still stopping.

LVGL is served by a thread, and the variant enables the MicroPython GIL so that this thread and main.py or the REPL never call LVGL at the same time (see docs/stm32mp135f-dk.md).

Both this driver and touch_evdev.py are frozen. Keep .frozen at the start of MICROPYPATH in the REPL services. Before a soft-reset execve, mpyrepl closes inherited descriptors above stderr so that DRM and input devices do not leak across restarts.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: tests/hil/t11_mp135_display.py checks the physical DRM panel, touch, backlight and stop()/start(); tests/hil/t12_mp135_performance.py measures full-screen rendering throughput.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Each example is an LVGL MPY Studio project (project.json, with its Python modules inside), made with the Studio's MCP tools. Open it in the Studio, try it in the simulator (demo data stands in for the network and the sound), connect to the board and run it. To have it in the home screen's menu, add it to settings.json, section home.

Each example has two projects with the same Python modules: project.json for 480×272 (STM32MP135F-DK) and project-800x480.json for 800×480 (STM32MP157C-DK2). Sizes drawn by the code follow the widgets, so the modules fit both.

Source: examples on GitHub.

docs.title: Weather
docs.text: Weather now and for the next five days from Open-Meteo (no account, no key), with icons drawn by LVGL objects from the WMO weather code: no image files. The settings page finds the place by name and sets the units, the update interval and the night: by default the backlight goes down to 20% from 23:00 to 05:30, in the place's own time. curl downloads in the background, so the screen never waits. Source

docs.title: Web radio
docs.text: Internet radio stations, built in or from a stations.txt. GStreamer's gst-play-1.0 plays the stream in the background through linuxproc.Process; the app connects to the Wi-Fi of the Settings app by itself. Needs a sound card: a USB audio adapter is enough. Source

docs.title: MP3 player
docs.text: The songs of the music folder, with titles and artists from their ID3 tags: play, pause, previous, next, volume, progress. The same player module as the radio. Source

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Wi-Fi: scan, choose, type the password on the touch keyboard, connect; and the layout of a keyboard plugged into the board. The choices go to settings.json, where every app finds it through mpy_settings and mpy_wifi.ensure(). Source

docs.title: Shell
docs.text: A terminal on the display, the home screen at power-on: built-in commands, the vi and edit editors, Python programs and Linux programs on a pseudo-terminal, with a USB keyboard plugged into the board or the keyboard of the serial or TCP terminal. A tap opens the app menu. Source

docs.title: machine: the hardware
docs.text: Apps that show MicroPython's machine API on a Linux board, in examples/machine. Their hardware code is the standard API, the same as on a microcontroller; on the STM32MP157C-DK2 Pin is served by Linux and the rest by the Cortex-M4.

docs.title: Board Explorer
docs.text: The Arduino connector on the screen: tap a pin, make it an input, an output, an analog input or the PWM, see its value live. The Cortex-M4 reads back the level of an output Linux drives and measures its own PWM on the pin; the LEDs come from Linux's LED class, machine.Pin and the M4. Nothing to wire. Source

docs.title: Oscilloscope
docs.text: One of A0 to A5 on a chart, 0.25 to 20 ms a division, triggered on an edge, with minimum, maximum, peak to peak, frequency and duty, and a 1 kHz test signal on D6: one wire from D6 to A0 and the square wave is on the screen. The Cortex-M4's TIM2 paces the conversions in hardware, up to 100,000 samples a second; Python starts a capture, collects it when it is done and draws it, so the screen never waits. (Above: the Studio simulator.) Source

docs.title: Timing Lab
docs.text: Something every 10 ms, three ways: a Python thread that sleeps, machine.Timer callbacks, and the expiries the Cortex-M4 counts. A histogram shows the intervals; a switch loads Linux with two busy processes. Measured: even idle, Linux stretches some intervals to tens of milliseconds (the GIL while the screen is drawn), loaded to over 100 ms; the M4's count stays whole, with no drift. What must happen at an exact time belongs on the M4. Nothing to wire. Source

docs.title: Logic Analyzer
docs.text: The board watches its own buses, no wires: the Cortex-M4 samples GPIO port E at up to 4 MHz while it sends a UART message, an SPI transfer or the PWM, started with the capture; Python decodes them (UART 8N1, SPI mode 0, PWM) and draws one row a pin, the bytes over their frames. Source

docs.title: Web Panel
docs.text: The board serves a page to the phones of its network: scan the QR code, type the PIN on the screen, see A0 to A5 live, switch the LEDs, set the PWM, send a message to the board's screen, which shows what each browser did. A few lines of MicroPython, polled from the GUI's timer: about 16 ms a request. (Above: the Studio simulator.) Source

docs.title: Data Logger
docs.text: The CPU's temperature (Linux), A0 and the chip's reference (the Cortex-M4), at the pace of an M4 timer, into a CSV file dated by the network's clock, on a chart, and for a browser to download. Each part where it is best: the M4 keeps the pace, Linux keeps the files and the time. Source

docs.title: Tone Player
docs.text: A keyboard on the screen and tunes the Cortex-M4 plays by itself, on time, on D6 (a passive buzzer): Python hands over the whole score and lights each key as the M4 plays it. Without a buzzer the M4 measures each note on the pin. Source

docs.title: System Monitor
docs.text: The board's two halves live: Linux's cores, memory, temperature and network from its own files, and the Cortex-M4's state, firmware, channel and the time of a request there and back. Source

docs.title: Phase 0 reconnaissance: STM32MP135F-DK, Linux, MicroPython and LVGL
docs.text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Scope: the no-hardware reconnaissance defined by the project plan. No board was flashed or contacted. No upstream source was modified.

This is a personal project by Nunzio Raciti and is not affiliated with or endorsed by STMicroelectronics.

docs.title: 1. Outcome and decisions still required
docs.text:
The selected starting release is Yocto-based OpenSTLinux ecosystem v6.2.1, confirmed by Nunzio on 2026-11-17. It is the current release on the official wiki and explicitly supports STM32MP135F-DK. No published v7 ecosystem release was found during this reconnaissance.

The host test shows that MicroPython v1.29.0 unix already provides the normal REPL, raw REPL, raw-paste and the filesystem operations needed by mpremote when the connection uses resume. It does not emulate an MCU soft reset: Ctrl-D terminates the process, without printing soft reboot, and the default mpremote command sequence therefore fails. Phase 4 must add and test process supervision, reset-mode restoration and boot/application startup. The final choice among options A, B and C remains open pending that spike and Nunzio's approval.

The studio analysis also identified two integration requirements that must not be overlooked:

  • The board driver must implement display_driver contract 1. The old init(), poll(), tick() and wait() interface belongs to the legacy/simulator path, not to current board application generation.
  • Absolute paths such as /lms_apps are real Linux absolute paths on the unix port. A systemd WorkingDirectory alone does not map them below /usr/local/mpy/fs. Phase 4/6 must either provide explicit filesystem confinement or use a reviewed board-profile path mapping.

docs.text:
• Verified by execution: a command was run on this host and its output is reported below.
  • Read: information comes from the cited source code or official documentation.
  • Inferred: a consequence of verified/read facts; it still needs an implementation test.
  • Deferred to hardware: cannot be verified until the corresponding board phase.

docs.title: 4. Flash and boot procedure for Phase 1
4.1 Hardware connections and switches (read)
docs.text:
• SW1 selects the boot mode. The table columns are Boot 0, Boot 1 and Boot 2.
  • USB/UART programming: 0 0 0.
  • microSD boot: 1 0 1.
  • On SW1, 0 means OPEN; 1 means the other/closed position.
  • Flash through CN7 / USB_OTG, the USB Type-C flashload and dual-role-port connector.
  • Power through CN12, USB Type-C, 5 V / 3 A.
  • Keep the Linux console on CN10, USB Micro-B ST-LINK/V3E. It must not become the MicroPython REPL channel.

Source: STM32MP135x-DK hardware description.

docs.title: 4.2 Commands (read; execute only at the hardware checkpoint)
docs.text:
Run from the images/stm32mp1 directory of the extracted Starter Package.

Linux:

STM32_Programmer_CLI -l usb
STM32_Programmer_CLI -c port=usb1 \
  -w flashlayout_st-image-weston/optee/FlashLayout_sdcard_stm32mp135f-dk-optee.tsv

Windows uses the same arguments with STM32_Programmer_CLI.exe. The USB index must be taken from the actual -l usb output rather than assumed if more than one DFU device is present.

Phase 1 host check on 2026-11-17: STM32_Programmer_CLI.exe --version ran successfully and reported 2.22.0. The tool must be updated to the release-validated 2.23.0 before flashing; the older installed version was not used.

After flashing, power/reset as directed by ST, set SW1 to microSD (1 0 1) and boot. The expected startup sequence is U-Boot splash, Linux splash, Weston and the GTK demo launcher. The expected host console command is:

picocom -b 115200 /dev/ttyACM0

The host device name, the board-side console name and the successful boot are deferred to hardware. Do not assume ttySTM0 without checking the board inventory.

docs.title: 5.2 How the studio communicates with a normal board (read)
docs.text:
For every adapter except stm32h7_uart, DeviceSession invokes python -m mpremote. The STM32H7 adapter instead uses the studio's own UartTransport; that adapter is not the model to select for this Linux board.

Important operations:

Studio action Command or transport behavior Connect break_in(port), then the device-information raw-REPL probe Execute source mpremote connect PORT resume exec SOURCE Reset mpremote connect PORT soft-reset, then a 0.5 s host sleep Upload one file mpremote connect PORT fs cp LOCAL :REMOTE (no resume) Read one file mpremote connect PORT resume fs cp :REMOTE LOCAL Run generated app raw-REPL exec which inserts the app directory in sys.path and imports app_main Stop app raw-REPL exec which removes app modules and calls display_driver.stop() Interactive REPL mpremote connect PORT repl Console direct mpremote.transport_serial.SerialTransport, with a continuous reader

Before a standard connection, break_in() writes \r\x03, then \x03, then \x03, with 0.3 s pauses. With resume, mpremote's raw entry writes \r\x03, flushes pending input and writes \r\x01. It expects:

raw REPL; CTRL-B to exit\r\n>

Raw-paste starts with \x05A\x01. A supporting target answers R\x01, followed by the little-endian flow-control window and window-availability bytes. Execution ends with Ctrl-D; the response contains OK, stdout, Ctrl-D, stderr, Ctrl-D and >.

Without resume, mpremote enters raw mode and immediately sends Ctrl-D. It requires soft reboot\r\n, followed by another raw-REPL banner. This exact behavior explains the failed standard commands in section 7 and is a mandatory compatibility requirement for Phase 4.

Upload generates and syntax-checks the application, probes firmware capabilities, soft-resets, writes into <app>.uploading, verifies remote file sizes, rotates the previous app to .previous, renames staging into place and optionally imports app_main. File copies without resume may themselves request a soft reset, so reset handling must work repeatedly during one upload, not only from the explicit Restart action.

Sources: lvgl_mpy_studio/device/service.py, lvgl_mpy_studio/device/uart.py, and mpremote 1.29.0 transport_serial.py and commands.py.

docs.title: 5.3 Board-profile contract (read)
docs.text:
A profile is schema version 1 and includes:

  • id, name, revision and one registered adapter;
  • minimum MicroPython/LVGL versions and required modules;
  • physical/logical width and height, scale, RGB565 and orientation [0];
  • optional font list;
  • config.driver="display_driver", config.buffers="driver" and config.eventLoop="driver";
  • optional appRoot, mainPath and touch configuration.

The serial port is a local user preference, not a profile field. The current adapter registry contains only waveshare_rgbpanel, stm32h7_uart and esp32_4848s040. Phase 6 therefore needs a reviewed Linux adapter/profile change; reusing an MCU adapter name would be misleading.

The default app root is /lms_apps, and the default autostart path is /main.py. The STM32H7 profile instead uses /flash/lms_apps and /flash/main.py. On this target the final mapping must be consistent with /usr/local/mpy/fs and with actual unix path semantics.

machine.unique_id() is optional during the initial information probe but mandatory for autostart transactions. The standard unix port does not provide an MCU machine identity. A stable, reviewed identity solution is therefore required before enabling studio autostart.

mpremote supports socket connections, but the studio's direct console is serial-specific and break_in() uses pyserial. TCP upload/exec may be feasible while full console support is not; this must be tested and, if needed, fixed in the studio in Phase 6 rather than hidden in the board firmware.

docs.title: 5.4 Display driver contract used by generated board apps (read)
docs.text:
The current contract is CONTRACT = 1 and is documented in this repository in docs/display-driver.md. The required public names are:

CONTRACT, WIDTH, HEIGHT, BUFFERS, PERIOD_MS, indev
start(), stop(), running(), backlight(percent=None)

Importing display_driver initializes LVGL, display and touch and starts background LVGL service. The generated app_main.py checks resolution, imports ui and app_events, loads the initial screen, calls display_driver.start() and returns. It does not own an event loop.

The simulator's contract-1 driver (runtime/program/display_driver.py) uses:

  • one full-screen RGB565 bytearray;
  • lv.DISPLAY_RENDER_MODE.DIRECT;
  • a 5 ms background service;
  • lv.tick_inc() followed by lv.timer_handler() in that service;
  • a pointer indev fed by the simulator;
  • idempotent start() and stop(), with the last frame retained on stop.

The older runtime/display_driver.py and project_gen.py legacy path use init(), poll(), tick(), wait() and an application-owned loop. They are not the interface to implement for new board-generated applications.

Each test launched a fresh standard unix binary behind a raw PTY, equivalent to:

  EXEC:$PWD/work/micropython/ports/unix/build-standard/micropython,pty,stderr,onlcr=0 &

docs.title: 7.1 Default mpremote behavior
docs.text:
Each command below was also rerun with a fresh process so that an earlier exit could not affect the next result.

Command Exit Result mpremote connect /tmp/upy exec "print(1+1)" 1 Fails waiting for soft reboot; unix exits and the PTY returns EIO mpremote connect /tmp/upy fs ls 1 Same automatic-soft-reset failure mpremote connect /tmp/upy soft-reset 1 Same missing soft-reboot emulation

The final host-side error was OSError: [Errno 5] Input/output error. The underlying cause is visible in ports/unix/main.c and shared/runtime/pyexec.c: Ctrl-D returns a forced-exit result, main() deinitializes and returns; no soft reboot message or in-process reset exists.

docs.title: 7.2 Commands with resume
docs.text:
Command Exit Observed output/result ... connect /tmp/upy resume exec "import sys; print(1+1); print(sys.platform)" 0 2 and linux ... connect /tmp/upy resume fs ls 0 Listing of the process working directory ... connect /tmp/upy resume fs cp tests/hil/phase0-hello.py :phase0-hello.py 0 Copy completed ... connect /tmp/upy resume fs cat :phase0-hello.py 0 Exact test source printed

A direct SerialTransport check entered raw mode with soft_reset=False and executed print(6*7). Output was 42, and transport.use_raw_paste remained True. This verifies the raw-paste path rather than a fallback to normal raw REPL.

docs.title: 7.3 Consequences for Phase 4
docs.text:
Verified: upstream raw REPL, raw-paste and filesystem commands work when no automatic reset is requested. Verified: upstream alone does not meet the soft-reset protocol.

Inferred, still requiring a spike: a process supervisor may be able to preserve the serial endpoint, print the expected reset banner, restart immediately in raw mode and run the system boot/application hooks. It must also survive repeated resets during studio upload. If that contour cannot meet the byte protocol and timing reliably, the C-module option remains the next candidate. No final A/B/C selection is made by this document.

Not tested in Phase 0: board USB gadget behavior, TCP transport, boot.py/main.py automation, safe mode, Ctrl-C during a graphical app, 200 KB throughput, reset latency, stress cycles, RSS stability, mpremote mount, Windows hardware behavior or any display/touch function.

docs.title: STM32MP135F-DK installation and recovery
docs.text:
This guide installs the MicroPython/LVGL binary, the USB NCM+CDC-ACM gadget, the REPL hub and the MCU-style REPL on OpenSTLinux 6.6-yocto-scarthgap-mpu-v26.06.10. The instructions are specific to the validated STM32MP135F-DK/MB1635 configuration. Do not apply the DTB to another board or another OpenSTLinux release.

The ST-LINK virtual COM port remains the Linux console. The MicroPython REPL uses the separate USB-C gadget CDC-ACM port or TCP over USB networking.

docs.title: Build on the development host
docs.text:
Install the matching OpenSTLinux Developer Package SDK, then run:

cd /opt/devel/lvgl/lvgl-mpy-linux
scripts/build_mp135.sh lvgl
scripts/build_mp135_usb.sh
REV=$(git describe --always --dirty)

The required files are:

  • dist/micropython-STM32MP135F_DK-lvgl-$REV
  • dist/stm32mp135f-dk-usb-composite-$REV.dtb

Each has a SHA-256 file. build_mp135_usb.sh refuses an unexpected base DTB and checks the final TX FIFO layout. Use scripts/build_mp135.sh minimal instead of lvgl only when LVGL is not wanted.

docs.title: Prepare SSH access
docs.text:
The installation runs over SSH with a key. Set it up once through the ST-LINK Linux console (picocom -b 115200 /dev/ttyACM0 on Linux, the ST-LINK COM port on Windows). Root's home is /home/root, not /root:

install -d -m 0700 /home/root/.ssh
# put the public key in /home/root/.ssh/authorized_keys, then:
chmod 0600 /home/root/.ssh/authorized_keys

Only after SSH with the key has been verified, disable password authentication by setting this in /etc/default/dropbear:

DROPBEAR_EXTRA_ARGS=" -s"

Restart dropbear.socket after changing that file. The installation scripts do not change SSH. Before the first installation the board is reachable over the original ST USB network gadget at 192.168.7.1.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
From the repository root, after the build:

scripts/deploy.sh            # BOARD defaults to 192.168.7.1

deploy.sh copies the newest MicroPython binary, mpy-repl-hub and DTB from dist/ (select others with MICROPYTHON=, HUB=, DTB=), the launcher, the units and the scripts of linux/ to /tmp/mpy-install on the board, and runs linux/install.sh there. install.sh:

  • checks that the board is an STM32MP135F-DK and that every file matches its SHA-256;
  • copies only what differs, through a temporary name, so a running program is never overwritten;
  • keeps the original DTB once as /boot/stm32mp135f-dk.dtb.st-original;
  • installs /etc/default/usbotg, which disables the original ST gadget startup so that it cannot race the composite NCM+ACM gadget;
  • removes the units of earlier installations (one TCP REPL process per connection);
  • disables Weston, psplash-drm-start.service (it holds DRM master) and st-hostname.service (it appends a MAC suffix to the hostname), and sets the hostname to mp135-mpy (MPY_HOSTNAME= to change it, empty to leave it);
  • enables mpy-usb-composite.service and mpy-repl.service;
  • says whether a reboot is needed (new DTB or no gadget yet), restarts the REPL when only programs changed, or reports that nothing changed.

The uninstaller is installed as /usr/local/mpy/bin/mpy-uninstall. Run deploy.sh again after every build: an unchanged installation reports nothing changed.

On Windows, scripts/deploy.sh runs from Git Bash with the OpenSSH client of Windows. Without Bash, copy the files listed at the top of linux/install.sh to a folder on the board (for example with scp from PowerShell) and run sh install.sh there.

The expected DTB SHA-256 values for this exact release are:

bf08a8e8aa6e0e2aacb1e37d76e1045c4702aff2239b8ff32234369b7235c294  original
0c0e3d98a814a9f394056e74c914e00f0ce96b926108d60d55be9e71ee9da2f9  NCM+ACM, B1 on PA14

After boot, the board has 192.168.7.1/24 on usb0; the host address is assigned dynamically. Both units should be active and the panel shows "MicroPython ready" while there is no main.py:

systemctl is-active mpy-usb-composite.service mpy-repl.service
systemctl --failed

The REPL service uses MICROPYPATH=.frozen:/usr/local/mpy/fs:/usr/local/mpy/fs/lib. The .frozen entry is required for display_driver, touch_evdev and mpy_ready, which are compiled into the binary. A soft reset re-executes /proc/self/exe; install.sh restarts the service after replacing the binary, so no process keeps running the old one.

docs.title: Connect and test
docs.text:
Install mpremote and pyserial on the host. On Linux, identify the new gadget port rather than reusing the ST-LINK console; in the validated setup it was /dev/ttyACM2.

P=/dev/ttyACM2
mpremote connect $P exec "import sys; print(sys.platform)"
mpremote connect $P fs ls
mpremote connect socket://192.168.7.1:8266 fs ls

The name that does not change is in /dev/serial/by-id/: usb-Copper-And-Code_MicroPython_LVGL_*.

On a PC with ModemManager (most Linux desktops), install the board's udev rule once. Without it, ModemManager takes the board's serial port for a modem whenever the board starts and sends it AT commands; while it probes, the port echoes the board's output back as input, and the shell on the screen runs that text as commands (AT: command not found) and may leave:

sudo cp linux/host/70-mpy-lvgl-board.rules /etc/udev/rules.d/
sudo udevadm control --reload

Run the full HIL test only after backing up any existing :main.py, because the test temporarily replaces it and removes it during cleanup:

P=$P TCP=socket://192.168.7.1:8266 tests/hil/test_repl.sh

Run the physical display checks and the 10-second full-screen benchmark from this repository root:

mpremote connect $P run tests/hil/t11_mp135_display.py
mpremote connect $P run tests/hil/t12_mp135_performance.py

To upload and run the interactive Studio example, use the matching Studio executable and board profile stm32mp135f_dk_480x272:

/opt/devel/lvgl/lvgl-mpy-studio/.venv/bin/lvgl-mpy-studio --language en device run \
    examples/stm32mp135f-dk/project.json --port $P

The panel shows a dark page with a TOUCH ME button. A successful press changes the label to Touch works! and prints STM32MP135_TOUCH_OK on the REPL console. The same project can be opened in the Studio GUI; connect to the CDC-ACM gadget port, not the ST-LINK Linux console.

On Windows, identify the new CDC-ACM COM port in Device Manager and install the Python packages with py -m pip install mpremote pyserial. The individual commands accept P=COM<n> and the same socket address. The Bash HIL script can run from Git Bash with native Windows Python tools on PATH; it uses cygpath for fixture paths. The Windows checkpoint is still pending.

The TCP REPL has no authentication or encryption and listens only on 192.168.7.1:8266. Do not expose it on Ethernet, Wi-Fi or an untrusted network without a separate security design. Serial and TCP reach the same MicroPython process; as with dupterm on the MCU ports, two clients typing at once see each other's output.

docs.title: Install the shell-linux application
docs.text:
The optional examples/shell-linux application adds the ANSI shell, edit, vi and Linux program execution on a PTY. Install its runtime modules in /usr/local/mpy/fs and the two Python editors in /usr/local/mpy/fs/bin:

ssh root@$BOARD 'install -d /usr/local/mpy/fs/bin'
scp examples/shell-linux/shell_linux.py examples/shell-linux/ansiterm.py \
    examples/shell-linux/ansifont.py examples/shell-linux/OFL.txt \
    root@$BOARD:/usr/local/mpy/fs/
scp examples/shell-linux/edit.py examples/shell-linux/vi.py \
    root@$BOARD:/usr/local/mpy/fs/bin/

Start it from the MicroPython REPL with:

import shell_linux
shell_linux.main()

The application is not added to main.py by default. See examples/shell-linux/README.md for command lookup, the linux override, Ctrl-C behavior, tests and current pipeline/exit-status limitations. Linux commands inherit the REPL service's root privileges.

docs.title: Working from afar: screenshots and taps
docs.text:
Two tools let a board be checked and driven without looking at it or touching it:

scripts/screen.sh screen.png          # what the panel shows now, turned as the user sees it
scripts/tap.sh 400 300                # a tap at screen coordinates (x, y)

mpy-screenshot (tools/mpy-screenshot/, installed in /usr/local/mpy/bin) reads the framebuffer the display controller shows through DRM and writes a PNG; it does not disturb the program that draws it or the REPL. mpy_tap.py writes a press and a release into the touchscreen's own event device, turned back from screen to panel coordinates, so display_driver reads them as a finger. Both need root. With two boards at the same address, set MPY_SSH_ALIAS as for scripts/deploy.sh.

docs.title: Uninstall and recovery
docs.text:
To return to the original OpenSTLinux configuration (original DTB and USB gadget, Weston and the demo), run on the board and reboot:

/usr/local/mpy/bin/mpy-uninstall            # --purge also removes /usr/local/mpy
reboot

The board is then reachable again over the original ST USB network gadget at 192.168.7.1; running scripts/deploy.sh installs everything again.

If the board does not boot or the USB gadget fails, use the ST-LINK Linux console and do the same by hand:

cp /boot/stm32mp135f-dk.dtb.st-original /boot/stm32mp135f-dk.dtb
systemctl disable --now mpy-repl.service mpy-usb-composite.service
rm -f /etc/default/usbotg
reboot

docs.title: Safe-mode validation
docs.text:
B1/USER1 is PA14, active-low with a pull-up, device-tree key BTN_1 (0x101). B2/USER2 is PA13 and is exposed separately as BTN_2 (0x102). The DTB overlay disables the blue heartbeat LED because it shares PA14 with B1. The launcher checks B1 through /dev/input/by-path/platform-gpio-keys-event and skips main.py when pressed.

Physical validation observed three complete BTN_1 press/release cycles. A normal service restart executed the temporary main.py marker; holding B1 during another service restart printed Safe mode: main.py skipped and did not execute the marker. Releasing B1 returned mpyrepl.user_button_pressed() to false. B2's mechanical switch on the validation board was damaged by a knock and is to be replaced; B2 was not tested.

To enter safe mode, hold B1 while restarting mpy-repl.service, then release it after the message. Do not hold B1 during a full board reset unless the U-Boot USB programming mode is intended.

docs.title: Phase 2 configuration and installation notes
docs.text: These are the approved board changes to preserve when creating the final user installation guide and installer. They are not yet a complete installation procedure.

docs.title: Network and SSH
docs.text:
• CN7/USB_OTG provides the existing NCM interface usb0; no gadget replacement is required.
  • The board has 192.168.7.1/24 and runs a DHCP server on this interface. The development host received 192.168.7.58/24; this host address is dynamic and must not be hard-coded.
  • SSH is provided by dropbear.socket, not OpenSSH. The key-only configuration was verified after a reboot; an attempt without the public key was rejected.
  • Root's actual home is /home/root, not /root. The authorized key must therefore be installed as /home/root/.ssh/authorized_keys, with mode 0600 and parent directory mode 0700.
  • The selected host public key is id_rsa.pub, fingerprint SHA256:Qak5m6jc+Adn/q9ouKuO/q9Yd2lnJzq4f0c9ocACwrU.
  • /etc/default/dropbear contains DROPBEAR_EXTRA_ARGS=" -s" to disable SSH password authentication. The local root password was not changed.
  • /etc/hosts maps 127.0.1.1 to mp135-mpy.

docs.title: Services and hostname
docs.text:
The following units were explicitly approved and disabled:

systemctl disable --now weston-graphical-session.service weston-checkgpu.service seatd-weston.service
systemctl disable st-hostname.service
hostnamectl set-hostname mp135-mpy

st-hostname.service must remain disabled for this configuration: its original /usr/bin/st-hostname.sh script appends the end0 MAC suffix to a hostname on every boot. The script itself was not modified. All other services, including networking, Dropbear and the USB gadget, remain enabled.

After the first reboot, all three Weston units were disabled and inactive, no systemd units were failed, and Nunzio confirmed a black panel with no ST demo. SSH remained available. A static OpenSTLinux boot logo can remain visible on later boots; without Weston it has no touch handling and is not an interactive application.

docs.title: Phase 3 cross-build and on-board validation
docs.text:
The x86-64 Developer Package SDK archive SDK-x86_64-stm32mp1-openstlinux-6.6-yocto-scarthgap-mpu-v26.06.10.tar.gz was extracted and its installer completed successfully. The installed environment reports GCC 13.4.0, ARCH=arm, CROSS_COMPILE=arm-ostl-linux-gnueabi- and the expected OECORE_SDK_VERSION.

The SDK and board both provide libffi 3.4.6, so MICROPY_PY_FFI=1 is retained. They also provide libdrm 2.4.120 and SDL2 2.30.1, but the final MicroPython binaries do not link SDL. The SDK environment does not export SIZE; the build script therefore sets SIZE, STRIP and READELF explicitly with the cross-tool prefix.

Reproducible builds use scripts/build_mp135.sh. It builds mpy-cross for the host before loading the SDK environment and pins MicroPython v1.29.0, lvgl-micropython 58d18ce and lvgl-bindings 7740c2f (LVGL 9.5.0). The validated commands in this development workspace are:

cd /opt/devel/lvgl/lvgl-mpy-linux
scripts/build_mp135.sh minimal
scripts/build_mp135.sh lvgl

WORK_DIR defaults to work/ inside this repository and can be set to another workspace; SDK_DIR defaults to the matching SDK directory below it. Outputs and SHA-256 files are written to dist/.

Build text data bss Total Minimal 401,870 1,144 2,060 405,074 bytes LVGL 1,134,629 2,396 2,152 1,139,177 bytes

Both are stripped ARM EABI5 32-bit executables using /lib/ld-linux-armhf.so.3. The Phase 3 dynamic NEEDED entries were libm.so.6, libffi.so.8 and libc.so.6; Phase 5 adds libdrm.so.2 to the LVGL build for the DRM panel backend.

On the board, the LVGL binary reports MicroPython 1.29.0, sys.platform=linux, build STM32MP135F_DK and LVGL 9.5.0. The existing PyDevices fake-display smoke test, tests/hil/t02_lvgl_smoke.py, passes twice including after lv.deinit(); the second scene renders successfully and the MicroPython heap returns to its initial value. Output is in docs/log/stm32mp135f-dk-phase3-smoke.txt.

The fast official basics suite ran on the board: 545 tests performed, 544 passed and 28 skipped. Three tests requiring the optional, non-frozen unittest package were explicitly excluded. The only failure, int_64_basics.py, is a 32-bit reference mismatch: the board's 32-bit CPython raises OverflowError while creating the expected output, whereas MicroPython completes the test. The full output and diff are in docs/log/stm32mp135f-dk-phase3-tests-basics.txt.

PyDevices reports that this build does not include the optional jpegio module: JPEG images will not draw, while PNG and LVGL BIN remain available. JPEG support was not required for this phase.

docs.title: Phase 4 MCU-style REPL
docs.text:
The ST-LINK virtual COM port remains the Linux console. MicroPython uses the CDC-ACM function added to the existing USB gadget, preserving NCM networking, DHCP and SSH. On the validated host the gadget is /dev/ttyACM2, but the number is dynamic; the ST-LINK console must not be selected. The board-side device is /dev/ttyGS0. The REPL filesystem root is /usr/local/mpy/fs.

The composite gadget requires the TX FIFO layout supplied by linux/stm32mp135f-dk-usb-composite.dtso. scripts/build_mp135_usb.sh verifies the exact original DTB hash, applies the overlay and validates the resulting layout. Do not rebind the gadget while it is active: install the DTB and reboot. The original and modified DTB SHA-256 values are respectively bf08a8e8aa6e0e2aacb1e37d76e1045c4702aff2239b8ff32234369b7235c294 and 1f8a0bdafc669ee05ca19c3fda920df197a1503ca4471b5d4a305bc99884d939.

The board-specific mpyrepl user C module calls the upstream friendly/raw REPL implementations, executes boot.py and main.py, preserves the REPL mode and restarts in place with execve on soft reset. A linker wrapper around mp_hal_set_interrupt_char() enables terminal ISIG only while code runs. This is required for Ctrl-C in both normal raw REPL and raw-paste execution; no upstream MicroPython source is modified.

Requirement Validated result Friendly banner and >>> prompt Pass Ctrl-A / Ctrl-B raw/friendly switching Pass Ctrl-C during mpremote run raw-paste execution Pass; KeyboardInterrupt and REPL available Ctrl-D soft reset Pass; raw mode restored and main.py executed Filesystem : rooted at /usr/local/mpy/fs Pass; copy, list, import and delete tested main.py exception Pass; traceback shown and REPL remains available B1 safe mode skips main.py Pass: three BTN_1 cycles; safe-mode marker observed and temporary main.py skipped TCP REPL on 192.168.7.1:8266 Pass; command, filesystem and soft reset tested

tests/hil/test_repl.sh automates the serial checks, the real main.py crash and TCP smoke tests. It temporarily replaces :main.py and removes it on completion or failure; back up any user application before running it. Example:

P=/dev/ttyACM2 TCP=socket://192.168.7.1:8266 tests/hil/test_repl.sh

Set MPREMOTE and PYTHON if they are not on PATH. Set TCP= to skip TCP. For Git Bash on Windows, use P=COM<n>; fixture paths are converted with cygpath. The Windows checkpoint has not yet been run.

Performance and stability measured on the board:

Test Result Soft reset to raw prompt, 10 samples min 0.060 s, mean 0.068 s, max 0.073 s Raw-paste copy of 204,800 bytes 11.778 s, 17.0 KiB/s, copied size verified 50 copy + soft-reset cycles No errors; one PID throughout Process RSS during stress 1,524–1,804 KiB; delta 280 KiB mpremote mount . exec ... Pass; host directory visible as /remote Two complete reboots NCM, SSH, ACM and TCP recovered; final boot had no failed units or FIFO/Oops errors

A standalone mpremote mount . mounts the directory and then enters the interactive REPL, so it needs a terminal; a non-interactive shell should append a command such as exec as shown above.

While code runs the CDC-ACM terminal has ISIG on for Ctrl-C only: Ctrl-Z and Ctrl-\ are disabled, both by the service stty and by mpyrepl, so they cannot stop or kill the REPL process. StartLimitIntervalSec=0 keeps Restart=always working through a crash loop.

mpy-repl.service runs mpy-repl-hub (tools/mpy-repl-hub/): one MicroPython process on a pseudo-terminal, shared by the CDC-ACM port and one TCP client on 192.168.7.1:8266. The terminal's line discipline turns Ctrl-C into SIGINT for both channels. Output goes to both clients, as with MicroPython's dupterm on the MCU ports, and input from both reaches the REPL; a new TCP connection replaces the previous one. A client that stops reading for 1 s has its output dropped until it reads again, so a closed serial port never blocks the REPL. When MicroPython exits the hub starts it again. The TCP listener has no authentication or encryption and is bound only to the USB gadget address. Results: docs/log/stm32mp135f-dk-repl-hub.txt.

A keyboard plugged into the board (USB, or any evdev device with letter keys) is one more input of the hub (tools/mpy-repl-hub/keyboard.c): its keys become what a terminal sends, so it types into the REPL, the shell on the screen, vi and the Linux programs, and Ctrl-C interrupts as from the serial port. One plugged in later is found within a second. The hub grabs it (EVIOCGRAB): the kernel's console would otherwise get the keys too, and the login prompt on tty1, which nobody sees, would take them as a user name. Layouts: us and it (AltGr included), chosen in the Settings app ({"keyboard": {"layout": "it"}} in settings.json, read again when it changes) or, without it, by MPY_KEYBOARD in the unit; none leaves the keyboards alone. The shell on the screen draws ASCII only: accented letters and the euro reach the programs, but show as ?. On the STM32MP157C-DK2 tests/hil/test_keyboard.sh checks both layouts with a virtual keyboard (uinput): letters, Caps Lock, the symbols, cursor keys and history, Ctrl-C.

UM2993 maps B1/USER1 to PA14 and B2/USER2 to PA13. The original configuration exposed PA13 as BTN_1 and drove PA14 as the blue heartbeat LED, so B1 presses produced no input events. The DTB overlay now disables that LED, exposes B1/PA14 as BTN_1 (0x101) and preserves B2/PA13 as BTN_2 (0x102) through /dev/input/by-path/platform-gpio-keys-event. Three complete physical B1 press/release cycles were observed. Holding B1 during an mpy-repl.service restart printed Safe mode: main.py skipped and prevented the temporary main.py marker from running; the normal restart control executed it. B2's mechanical switch on the validation board was damaged by a knock and is to be replaced; B2 was not tested.

Logs are saved as docs/log/stm32mp135f-dk-phase4-hil.txt, docs/log/stm32mp135f-dk-phase4-performance.txt, docs/log/stm32mp135f-dk-phase4-stress.txt, docs/log/stm32mp135f-dk-phase4-reboot.txt and docs/log/stm32mp135f-dk-phase4-safe-mode.txt. docs.title: Phase 5 display, touch and Studio integration
docs.text:
The panel is driven directly through DRM/KMS on /dev/dri/card0; this board has no /dev/fb0. The board-specific linuxfb user C module creates and maps a 480×272 RGB565 dumb buffer with a 1,024-byte stride, sets the DPI-1 CRTC and copies LVGL dirty rectangles into it. Weston and psplash-drm-start.service must be disabled so that MicroPython can become DRM master. The LVGL binary therefore has libdrm.so.2 as an additional dynamic dependency.

python/linux/display_driver.py implements display-driver contract 1 with one 255 KiB full-screen buffer in DIRECT mode. Its service thread calls lv.timer_handler() every 5 ms, while the LVGL refresh timer is limited to 16 ms. The variant enables the MicroPython GIL (MICROPY_PY_THREAD_GIL := 1): the unix port has none by default, and without it the service thread and main.py or the REPL would call LVGL at the same time. With the GIL each LVGL call is atomic, as with the scheduled callbacks of the MCU ports; the full-screen animation measured 57.09 FPS (58.14 without the GIL). LVGL event handlers run in the service thread, so Ctrl-C does not stop a handler that never returns. stop() waits for the service thread to exit, preventing an immediate start() from creating overlapping service threads. Backlight control uses /sys/class/backlight/panel-backlight and defaults to 100%.

python/linux/touch_evdev.py discovers Goodix Capacitive TouchScreen by name in /proc/bus/input/devices; the event number is not fixed. It polls the numeric file descriptor and decodes the verified 16-byte ARM32 input_event records with llHHi. ABS_MT_POSITION_X/Y, ABS_X/Y, tracking ID and BTN_TOUCH are handled. X increases rightward and Y downward, so no axis swap or inversion is needed. The board's FileIO does not expose read1() and its os module does not expose read(). After polling, each read therefore requests exactly one 16-byte event: the kernel supplies a complete event without MicroPython waiting to fill a larger buffer. Input is delivered one SYN_REPORT frame at a time and the LVGL continue_reading flag drains frames queued in the driver or kernel. A quick press and release therefore remain two distinct LVGL states instead of collapsing into a release with no click. tests/host/test_touch_evdev.py covers this quick-tap regression, partial frames, queued motion and the restricted FileIO method surface; tests/hil/t15_mp135_touch.py provides a visible click counter and callback timing on the panel.

Both Python modules are frozen by the board manifest. The serial and TCP REPL services set MICROPYPATH=.frozen:/usr/local/mpy/fs:/usr/local/mpy/fs/lib; omitting .frozen makes display_driver unavailable to applications. On soft reset, mpyrepl closes inherited descriptors above stderr before execve, preventing DRM and input descriptors from accumulating across process restarts.

docs.title: shell-linux application
docs.text:
examples/shell-linux extends the board with a separate Linux-capable shell without modifying the portable examples/shell application. It provides the MicroPython file and text commands, the edit and vi editors, and Linux executable lookup. Built-ins take precedence over Python programs in /usr/local/mpy/fs/bin, which in turn take precedence over executables in the Linux PATH; the linux command forces Linux execution.

The board-specific linuxproc user C module starts each program with fork/execvp on a controlling PTY. It forwards serial keyboard input and terminal output, sets the 60x17 panel dimensions, handles non-blocking backpressure while continuing to drain output, and kills the whole process group if a MicroPython callback raises. MICROPY_PY_OS_DUPTERM is enabled for the shared panel/serial ANSI terminal. The terminal alternate screen saves character cells and redraws them on exit rather than duplicating the 255 KiB framebuffer, allowing both editors to run within the MicroPython heap.

Installation, usage, limitations and HIL commands are documented in examples/shell-linux/README.md and linked from docs/stm32mp135f-dk-install.md. Autostart is optional and is not installed by default.

docs.title: Portable machine API decision
docs.text:
The project will expose one MicroPython-compatible public machine API across Linux-only MPU boards and boards with a real-time MCU. User code should not change when the underlying hardware backend changes.

  • On STM32MP135F-DK and similar Linux-only boards, classes such as Pin, I2C, SPI, PWM, ADC and Timer will use kernel interfaces and drivers. Direct peripheral register access from Linux user space is not part of this design.
  • On MPU boards with a programmable MCU, an equivalent backend may communicate with MCU firmware through remoteproc and RPMsg/OpenAMP. Native MicroPython MCU ports should retain their existing machine API wherever possible.
  • Public method signatures, units, ranges, return values, exceptions and resource cleanup semantics should be shared across backends. Board-specific names, device discovery and capabilities must be kept out of application code.
  • Unsupported peripherals and operations must be reported explicitly rather than emulated silently. Board capabilities must be discoverable and documented.
  • API compatibility does not imply equivalent timing guarantees. Linux-only backends must not claim hard real-time behavior; future real-time control-loop offload requires a separate, explicitly defined API.
  • The different backends should run the same hardware-in-the-loop contract tests where the board provides the corresponding peripheral.

STM32MP135F-DK has no programmable real-time MCU. Its initial implementation will therefore use the Linux kernel backend. The first class is machine.Pin (modules/linuxmachine/), on the GPIO character device (uAPI v2): lines by kernel name (Pin("PA4")) or (chip, offset), modes IN, OUT, OPEN_DRAIN, pulls PULL_UP, PULL_DOWN, value(), on(), off(), toggle(), init(), deinit(). A line used by the kernel raises OSError(EBUSY); irq() is not provided. tests/hil/t17_mp135_pin.py checks names, errors, inputs with pulls and release without driving any line; tests/hil/t19_mp135_led.py drives the green LD7 and orange LD6 LEDs on the MCP23017 expander (Pin(("mcp23017", 14))), confirmed by eye. tests/hil/t18_mp135_pin_loopback.py checks push-pull and open drain with a jumper across CN8 pins 38 (PA5) and 40 (PA0). A released line keeps its last configuration, as a pin does on the MCU ports when its Pin object is deleted: an output stays an output. Results: docs/log/stm32mp135f-dk-machine-pin.txt. This section records an architectural decision; it does not imply that all of these classes are already implemented.

docs.title: Start-up and robustness
docs.text:
The launcher (linux/mpy_launcher.py) checks B1 for safe mode, then, when there is no main.py or in safe mode, shows the ready screen (python/linux/mpy_ready.py): "MicroPython ready", the CDC-ACM port and the TCP address from MPY_REPL_TCP. Any error of the display, and a Ctrl-C from a client connecting at that moment, only costs the ready screen: the REPL starts anyway. The screen writes the kernel uptime at which it was drawn to /run/mpy-ready.

mpy-repl.service is Type=notify with WatchdogSec=10: the hub pings systemd from its loop, and a hub that stops is restarted. This shows that the REPL is served; a MicroPython program that hangs is not detected, as on the MCU ports, where that is the job of machine.WDT (not implemented yet).

After a reboot the ready screen is drawn at about 32.7 s of kernel uptime, right after the hub starts. Most of that time passes before sysinit.target (udev, microSD partitions); shortening it means changing the image (phase 9). Results: docs/log/stm32mp135f-dk-phase7.txt.

docs.title: Differences from the MCU boards
docs.text:
What LVGL MPY Studio, mpremote and an application see, compared with the MicroPython MCU boards of mpy-lvgl-boards:

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
• Start-up is slow (about 33 s to the ready screen) because of the image: udev and the microSD partitions take about 16 s before sysinit.target. A smaller image is phase 9.
  • No vsync or page flip: fast full-screen animations can tear.
  • A MicroPython program that hangs is not detected by the systemd watchdog (it watches the hub); machine.WDT is not implemented.
  • The TCP REPL has no authentication; it listens only on the USB network.
  • mpremote fs cp over the CDC-ACM port is slow (about 17 KiB/s); over TCP it is about 13 times faster.
  • B2 was not tested: its switch on the validation board is damaged.
  • Power loss: /var/log, /var/tmp and /tmp are already in RAM in this image, and install.sh keeps the systemd journal in RAM explicitly (linux/journald-volatile.conf). The root filesystem and /usr/local (its own partition, which holds fs/) are writable ext4: a power cut while the Studio copies an application can still damage it. A read-only root is for phase 9.

docs.title: Home screen
docs.text:
install.sh writes a main.py that starts mpy_home (frozen), unless a main.py is already there (MPY_AUTOSTART=none skips it). At power-on the display shows the shell of examples/shell-linux (frozen too), with the keyboard of the serial or TCP terminal: built-in commands, the edit and vi editors in fs/bin, Python programs (name.py in fs/bin, or python file.py) and Linux programs.

A tap on the terminal opens the app menu: the LVGL MPY Studio apps listed in settings.json, section home ({"apps": [{"name": ..., "path": ".../app_main.py"}]}), Shell, and Power off, which asks first and then runs systemctl poweroff. An app starts in a fresh process (mpyrepl.restart(), a soft reset), so apps never share modules; a small home tab at the top centre brings the shell back the same way. Every soft reset stops the Linux programs the application started with linuxproc.Process (a radio stream does not go on playing).

LVGL MPY Studio and mpremote take the board as on the MCU ports: Ctrl-A on an empty shell line hands over to the raw REPL, and after a soft reset asked from the raw REPL main.py does not run. Results: docs/log/stm32mp135f-dk-home.txt.

docs.title: STM32MP157C-DK2
docs.text:
Second board of this project, and the first with a microcontroller beside Linux: its Cortex-M4 serves machine.I2C, ADC, PWM, SPI, UART and Timer to MicroPython on the Cortex-A7.

Status: OpenSTLinux flashed; our build installed with scripts/deploy.sh (the same MicroPython binary as the STM32MP135F-DK); shell, app menu and REPL working (serial and TCP); the 480×800 panel turned to 800×480 in software (about 50 full frames per second); Wi-Fi, weather and the web radio with sound through the board's codec; machine.Pin on Linux GPIO lines, machine.I2C, ADC, PWM, SPI, UART and Timer on the Cortex-M4. Bring-up log: docs/log/stm32mp157c-dk2-bringup.txt. Product page: https://www.st.com/en/evaluation-tools/stm32mp157c-dk2.html. Flashing and boot: Populate the target and boot the image on the ST wiki.

docs.title: machine on the Cortex-M4
docs.text:
import array
from machine import I2C, ADC, PWM, SPI, UART, Timer, Pin

i2c = I2C(5, freq=400000)        # Arduino D14 SDA / D15 SCL, 40-pin header pins 3 and 5
print(i2c.scan())
i2c.readfrom_mem(0x76, 0xD0, 1)  # a register, as on any MicroPython board

print(ADC("A0").read_uv())       # Arduino A0..A5, from 0 to 2.5 V
print(ADC(ADC.CORE_VREF).read_uv())
samples = array.array("H", bytes(2 * 1000))
ADC("A0").read_timed(samples, 10000)           # 1000 samples at exactly 10 kHz, by the M4

servo = PWM("D6", freq=50, duty_ns=1500000)   # TIM1 channel 1 on PE9, Arduino D6

spi = SPI(4, baudrate=8000000)                 # SCK D13, MISO D12, MOSI D11
cs = Pin("PE11", Pin.OUT, value=1)             # D10: a Linux GPIO line as chip select
cs(0); spi.read(3, 0x9F); cs(1)

gps = UART(7, 9600, timeout=1000)             # RX D0, TX D1
print(gps.readline())

Timer(0, period=500, callback=lambda t: print("tick"))

Pin("PA14", Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP).value()   # Pin stays on Linux GPIO lines, as on the STM32MP135F-DK
                                           # (PA14 is the USER1 button: as an input only, see below)

How it fits together:

  • Device tree. The m4-examples device tree gives the Cortex-M4 the Arduino connector's ADC, DAC, I2C5, SPI4, UART7, TIM1 and TIM2, and the orange LED; Linux keeps the display, touch, Wi-Fi, audio and USB. Linux only reserves those pins: the firmware sets them itself. It also gives the M4 the USER1 button's interrupt (PA14, shared with the green LED): Linux may read PA14 but not drive it (EIO).
  • Firmware (mcu/stm32mp157c-dk2/, built by scripts/build_m4.sh with arm-none-eabi-gcc, without STM32CubeIDE): STM32Cube HAL and OpenAMP from STM32CubeMP1 1.7.0, our main.c and the protocol. install.sh puts it in /lib/firmware/mpy_m4.elf.
  • Start. The first use of machine.I2C, ADC, PWM, SPI, UART or Timer loads the firmware through remoteproc if the M4 is off (about 0.6 s). A new firmware installed by deploy.sh takes over at once.
  • Events. The M4 can also speak unasked: a frame with sequence number 0 is an event (a timer's expiry). A thread of mpy_m4 reads the port while nobody makes requests; events read during a request are kept for later. Handlers run outside the port's lock, so a callback may use the M4 itself. Then Python acknowledges, and only then does the M4 send that timer's next event.
  • Link. Two RPMsg channels, the same frames on both: a raw one (rpmsg-raw, which Linux's rpmsg_char turns into /dev/rpmsgN by itself) and a virtual serial port (rpmsg-tty, /dev/ttyRPMSGN). mpy_m4 uses the raw one, through the C library (ffi), and falls back on the serial port; their numbers change when the M4 restarts, so it looks them up. Requests and answers carry a length, a sequence number and an errno: the protocol is in mcu/stm32mp157c-dk2/firmware/Inc/mpy_m4_protocol.h. A request takes about 0.3 ms there and back (see Latency below).
  • Python. mpy_m4 (frozen) has the classes; the frozen machine module takes the place of MicroPython's built-in one (an "extensible" module in v1.29), imports all of it from umachine and adds I2C, ADC, PWM, SPI, UART and Timer on a board with a Cortex-M4. On the STM32MP135F-DK nothing changes.

docs.title: Latency
docs.text:
What a request to the M4 costs, there and back (2000 to 3000 requests each, as installed):

idle: median / 99% / 99.9% two busy Linux processes: median / 99% / 99.9% ADC.read_u16(), raw channel (rpmsg_char, the default) 290 / 371 / 494 to 772 us 292 / 386 to 418 us / 5.8 to 6.9 ms ADC.read_u16(), serial port 316 / 411 to 467 us / 2.3 ms 316 / 503 to 1103 us / 9.9 ms a bare request on the raw channel, no mpy_m4 162 / 215 to 240 / 270 to 600 us 162 / 220 to 260 us / 7 to 9 ms a Linux GPIO line, Pin.value(), for comparison 8 us 8 us

About 3000 requests a second: plenty to command and read, 40 times a GPIO line, so the fast loops stay on the M4 (read_timed, mpy_m4.measure, a whole I2C scan in one request). The M4's own work is small (the slowest ADC conversion, 810.5 cycles, about 70 us); of the rest, about 160 us are Linux (system calls, the M4's interrupt, waking Python up) and about 70 us mpy_m4's Python.

What brought these numbers down, measured one step at a time:

  • mpy_m4 reads a whole answer in one poll() and one read(): about 10%.
  • mpy-repl.service runs MicroPython at real-time priority (SCHED_FIFO 10; the programs it starts through linuxproc at normal priority): under load the slowest 1% went from 8 ms to under 0.6 ms.
  • The raw channel goes around Linux's tty layer and its worker thread: 25 us less a request through mpy_m4, and a slowest 0.1% three to four times shorter when idle.

Left: under load, about one request in a thousand takes up to 10 ms. That is one tick of this kernel (CONFIG_HZ=100): it stays even with the load at the lowest priority, so it is not the load taking the CPU but a stage of the kernel waiting for its tick. Only another kernel (HZ 1000, PREEMPT_RT) would remove it; what must happen at an exact time runs on the M4 anyway.

docs.title: I2C
docs.text:
Bus 5 only (I2C(5), the default): SDA PA12, SCL PA11, on the Arduino connector (D14, D15) and on the 40-pin header (pins 3 and 5, GPIO2/GPIO3). 10 kHz to 1 MHz; the default is 400 kHz. The weak internal pull-ups keep an empty bus high; devices bring their own.

Method Behaviour scan() the addresses 0x08 to 0x77 that answer (3 ms for an empty bus at 400 kHz) writeto, writevto, readfrom, readfrom_into as on MicroPython; OSError(ENODEV) when no device answers the address readfrom_mem, readfrom_mem_into, writeto_mem addrsize 8 or 16 writeto(addr, reg, False) then readfrom(addr, n) the register read with a repeated start, for a register address of 1 or 2 bytes

Up to 400 bytes a transfer. Not there: the primitive operations (start, stop, readinto, write), 10-bit addresses.

docs.title: ADC
docs.text:
16 bits against the 2.5 V reference buffer (VREFBUF), which Linux turns on for the M4: inputs from 0 to 2.5 V, never more than 3.3 V. read_u16() and read_uv().

Name Pin Converter A0 ANA0 ADC1 input 0 A1 ANA1 ADC1 input 1 A2 PF14 ADC2 input 6 A3 PF13 ADC2 input 2 A4 PC3 ADC1 input 13 A5 PF12 ADC1 input 6 ADC.CORE_VREF internal reference, about 1.21 V ADC2 ADC.CORE_TEMP temperature sensor (a voltage; Linux gives the chip's temperature in /sys/class/thermal) ADC2

The names follow the board's schematic (the net names of user manual UM2534); the manual's table of Arduino pins has some rows shifted. Pin names (ADC("PF14")) work too.

Sampling at a fixed rate. adc.read_timed(buf, freq), as on the Pyboard but with the rate instead of a timer: up to 32768 samples at 1 Hz to 100 kHz. The M4's TIM2 (32 bits at 208.9 MHz) triggers each conversion in hardware and an interrupt stores it in the M4's memory, so the samples are evenly spaced whatever Linux does; Python sleeps meanwhile (the GUI and the timers go on) and then collects them, 200 at a time. array('H') gets 16-bit values, a bytearray their top 8 bits; afterwards adc.freq is the exact rate (TIM2's clock over its period) and adc.overruns the conversions lost (none so far). The sampling time is the longest that fits the rate (810.5 ADC cycles up to 10 kHz, 64.5 at 100 kHz). For a GUI that must not wait, the same in steps (not in MicroPython's API): adc.capture(count, freq) starts and returns the exact rate, adc.capture_done(), adc.capture_read(buf); the oscilloscope example draws from them.

Measured: VREFINT at 1 kHz, 10 kHz and 100 kHz averages 1.206 V; the times between the first and the last conversion give 1000.00 Hz, 9999.90 Hz and 99,989.4 Hz (TIM2's 208.9 MHz over 2089); 32768 samples at 100 kHz take 0.41 s with their collection (0.33 s of sampling); no overruns. A real signal without wires: Linux charges A2 (PF14) as a GPIO output, the capture turns the pin analog and samples it: 1.87 V, then a falling curve, about 12% less at each conversion, the same from 10 to 100 kHz: the ADC's own sampling capacitor takes the charge. (A pin the ADC reads must be analog: driven by Linux as an output, the M4 sees it toggle digitally, at 50.00 Hz, but the ADC does not.)

Checked on the board (tests/hil/test_m4.sh, nothing wired): VREFINT reads 1.203 to 1.216 V (datasheet 1.18 to 1.24 V; its factory calibration in OTP says 1.209 V), the six inputs convert, an empty I2C bus answers ENODEV. Not checked yet: a real I2C device and a known voltage on an input.

docs.title: PWM
docs.text:
TIM1 channel 1 on PE9, Arduino D6 (PWM("D6") or PWM("PE9")), the pin the device tree gives the M4 for it. The MicroPython API: freq(), duty_u16(), duty_ns(), init(), deinit(); a new frequency keeps the pulse width when it was set in nanoseconds, the share otherwise. A new duty takes effect at the next period, without a glitch. From 1 Hz up; the timer counts at 208.9 MHz, so the duty has 16 bits of resolution up to 3.2 kHz (about 11 bits at 100 kHz). invert is not supported.

mpy_m4.logic_capture(count, freq, port="E", spi=None, uart=None) samples a whole GPIO port (16 pins) up to 4 MHz on the M4's cycle counter, up to 32768 samples, and returns them with the exact rate; an SPI4 transfer or a UART7 message can start with it (fed by the sampling loop after the first 5%), so the board can watch its own buses: the logic analyser example.

mpy_m4.play([(hz, ms), ...]) has the M4 play up to 100 notes on D6 by itself, on time (0 Hz is a rest), while it answers other requests; mpy_m4.playing() tells which note: the tone player example.

mpy_m4.measure(pin, ms) has the M4 sample a pin for a while (about 8 million samples a second) and returns its frequency (whole periods between the first and the last rising edge: exact even in 30 ms) and the share of time it was high: that is how the tests check the PWM without instruments. Measured on PE9: 1 kHz 25% gives 1000.00 Hz 25.00%; 50 Hz 1.5 ms gives 50.00 Hz 7.50%; 100 kHz 30% gives 99,990 Hz (208.9 MHz / 2089) 29.95%; 0% and 100% are steady.

docs.title: SPI
docs.text:
SPI4: SCK PE12 (D13), MISO PE13 (D12), MOSI PE14 (D11), on the Arduino connector. SPI(4) with the MicroPython API: init(), deinit(), read(), readinto(), write(), write_readinto(), polarity, phase, firstbit (SPI.MSB, SPI.LSB); 8-bit frames only. The rate is the fastest not above the one asked: the 64 MHz kernel clock over 2, 4, ... 256, so 32 MHz down to 250 kHz. Transfers longer than 400 bytes go in pieces of 400.

The chip select is the program's, as on most MicroPython boards: PE11 (D10) is not used by Linux, so Pin("PE11", Pin.OUT) drives it through the kernel's GPIO lines, beside the SPI on the M4.

Checked without a device: during a transfer the M4 samples its own SCK and MOSI pins and rebuilds the bytes it sees at the sampling edges; in the four modes, MSB and LSB first, at 500 kHz, they are the bytes sent, with 2 edges a bit (the sampling keeps up to about 1 MHz). MISO reads 0xFF with its internal pull-up and 0x00 with the pull-down. 1024 bytes at 32 MHz take 1.4 ms (732 kB/s); a short transfer about 0.36 ms there and back. Not checked yet: a real SPI device.

docs.title: UART
docs.text:
UART7: RX PE7 (Arduino D0), TX PE8 (D1). UART(7, baudrate) with the MicroPython API: init(), deinit(), any(), read(), readinto(), readline(), write(), flush(), txdone(), sendbreak(), timeout and timeout_char (at least a character's time, as on MicroPython). 300 baud to 4 Mbaud; 7, 8 or 9 data bits (with parity 7 or 8), parity None, 0 (even) or 1 (odd), 1 or 2 stop bits. errors() (not in MicroPython) counts overruns, framing and parity errors.

The M4 receives and sends under interrupt, with a 4 KB buffer for what arrives and a 2 KB one for what goes out: bytes are not lost between two calls from Python, and write() returns while the M4 sends.

Checked without wires: in single-wire mode the TX pin also receives what it sends. 8N1, 7E2, 8O1 from 300 baud to 4 Mbaud come back intact; 3 KB (more than the 2 KB to send) too; readline(), the timeout (200 ms measured 200 ms), a break (read as 0x00 with a framing error). The M4 measures the rate on the pin while sending 0x55 (a square wave at half the rate): 0.14% under nominal at every rate, the same offset everywhere, well inside what a serial line tolerates. Not checked yet: a real device on the line.

docs.title: Timer
docs.text:
Timer(id, mode=Timer.PERIODIC, period=ms, callback=f) or freq=Hz, init(), deinit(), Timer.ONE_SHOT; 8 timers (0 to 7, or -1 for a free one), periods from 1 ms (up to 1000 Hz).

The M4 counts, Linux calls: the expiries are timed by the M4's clock and none is lost, while the callback runs on Linux, in mpy_m4's reader thread, when Linux gets to it (typically within a millisecond; a 10 ms timer's gaps have a median of 10.000 ms, single ones from 5 to 15 ms). Until Python has handled an event, the M4 sends no further one for that timer: it counts the expiries into the next, and the callback finds them in timer.missed (not in MicroPython's API, like timer.late_us, how late the M4 sent the event). So a busy Linux never piles events up.

As with MicroPython's soft callbacks, the callback waits while the main thread runs Python without a pause: the GIL of MicroPython's unix port is not fair, and a loop that never sleeps, waits or does I/O keeps it (the LVGL thread waits the same way). Measured at 1 kHz for 0.5 s of such a loop: a few calls, the rest in missed, the count right. Anything that must happen at an exact time belongs on the M4 itself, as the ADC's sampling at a fixed rate does.

docs.title: What the M4 has that is not used
docs.text:
Peripheral Why not DAC Its outputs PA4 and PA5 are the CC lines of the USB-C power connector (CN6), which tell the board what powers it; they do not reach the connectors. Left alone. DMA2 Not needed so far: an interrupt stores the samples up to 100 kHz. (TIM2 paces read_timed; machine.Timer uses the M4's cycle counter.) HASH, CRYP, CRC, RNG MicroPython on Linux has hashlib and os.urandom, the board /dev/hwrng.

Linux keeps every timer off, so TIM4 (D3, D5) and TIM12 (D9) could give more PWM outputs, once declared to the M4 in a device tree overlay. machine.WDT (/dev/watchdog) and Pin.irq (GPIO edge events) belong on the Linux side.
